forces: Tenor and orchestra; acoustic scoring unestablished
intro: “Recondita armonia” comes from Act I of Tosca. In a Roman church, the painter Cavaradossi works on a blonde Mary Magdalene while he thinks of the dark-haired Tosca, and he sings of the beauty of both women and of his love for Tosca. Caruso sings the aria.

sections.label: A · Cavaradossi’s aria, Tosca and Magdalene
sections.mNote: Cavaradossi compares Tosca with his painting of the Magdalene.

sections.label: B · Blue eyes and black
sections.mNote: The tenor compares the two women’s faces.

sections.label: C · Tosca alone in his thoughts
sections.mNote: The comparison becomes a declaration of love.

cues.title: Recondita armonia, opening
cues.text: “Recondita armonia di bellezze diverse” — “A hidden harmony of different beauties.” Cavaradossi’s painted Mary Magdalene has blonde hair and blue eyes. His lover, Floria Tosca, is dark-haired, and the tenor’s aria opens with the painter comparing the two.
cues.evidence: Illica and Giacosa, Tosca (1900), Act I, scene 3; La Scala libretto, pp. 2–3, including the description of the painting. https://www.teatroallascala.org/static/upload/tos/tosca-libretto-accessibile.pdf . Translation ours.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: The Marchesa Attavanti
cues.text: The blonde woman is the Marchesa Attavanti. Cavaradossi has watched her praying in Sant’Andrea della Valle and painted her without her knowing. She also comes to the church to hide clothes in the family chapel for her brother Angelotti’s escape.
cues.evidence: Illica and Giacosa, Tosca (1900), Act I, scenes 3 and 6; La Scala libretto, pp. 2 and 11. https://www.teatroallascala.org/static/upload/tos/tosca-libretto-accessibile.pdf

cues.title: Blue eyes, black eyes
cues.text: Cavaradossi speaks to the painting as though the woman were there: “Tu azzurro hai l’occhio, Tosca ha l’occhio nero” — “Your eyes are blue; Tosca’s are black.”
cues.evidence: Illica and Giacosa, Tosca (1900), Act I, Recondita armonia; La Scala libretto, p. 3. https://www.teatroallascala.org/static/upload/tos/tosca-libretto-accessibile.pdf . Translation ours; the words describe the aria’s central comparison.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Final lines of the aria
cues.text: Cavaradossi sings that art can bring different beauties together. The aria then closes on the line “Il mio solo pensier, Tosca, sei tu” — “My only thought, Tosca, is you.”
cues.evidence: Illica and Giacosa, Tosca (1900), Act I, final lines of Recondita armonia; La Scala libretto, p. 3. https://www.teatroallascala.org/static/upload/tos/tosca-libretto-accessibile.pdf . Translation ours; placed at the established closing section.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Composer who held a theatre audience through a scene of a woman at a window, then brought back a tune it had heard before.
facts: Lucca; Milan Conservatory, 1880–83, with Bazzini and Ponchielli
Giulio Ricordi · Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa · Giuseppe Adami and Renato Simoni
Twelve operas, counting Il trittico as three; a Mass, songs and chamber music
composer.background:
Puccini began at the organ. His family had supplied Lucca with church musicians for generations, and when his father Michele died in 1864, the five-year-old Giacomo was expected to continue the trade. He studied in the town, played in its churches and completed a Mass in 1880. In 1876, however, he had heard Verdi’s Aida in Pisa, and he turned to the theatre. A scholarship helped him into the Milan Conservatory, where Antonio Bazzini and Amilcare Ponchielli taught him composition. His graduation piece of 1883, Capriccio sinfonico, contains the music that later opened La bohème.

He submitted his first opera, Le Villi, to the Sonzogno competition on the last possible day, 31 December 1883; it did not receive a mention. The librettist Ferdinando Fontana arranged a private hearing at the journalist Marco Sala’s house, with Arrigo Boito among the guests. A subscription paid for a performance at Milan’s Teatro Dal Verme the following May. Giulio Ricordi bought the opera and commissioned another. Edgar, first performed at La Scala in 1889, was a failure that Puccini spent years trying to repair.
